Mechanical cloaks manipulate elastic responses to make objects indistinguishable from homogeneous surroundings.
Continuum mechanics equations are not form-invariant under general coordinate transformations, limiting traditional cloak design methods.
A large pre-computed database of metamaterial unit cells with diverse topologies and properties was created using topology optimization and stochastic shape perturbations.
The cloak design optimizes both topology and spatial distribution of stiffness tensor entries within the cloak region.
Unit cells are selected from the database to match optimized local properties and assembled via tiling optimization ensuring mechanical compatibility.
The method can cloak voids of arbitrary shapes and multiple voids simultaneously.
Relative displacement difference Δ is used to quantify cloaking performance, with lower values indicating better cloaking.
In a circular void example, the relative displacement difference was reduced from 17.2% (voided) to 4% (cloaked) in simulations.
Experimental 3D-printed structures validated numerical results, showing good agreement in displacement fields and Δ values.
The method works under various boundary conditions: displacement-free, pressure-free, pressure-sliding, dilating, and shearing.
Optimized cloaks exhibit a stiffness gradient increasing from the outer to inner boundary of the cloak.
Tiling optimization uses an energy-minimization approach solved by dual decomposition on a grid-like graph.
The approach can design cloaks without predefined cloaking boundaries, adapting topology to void geometry.
The method can aggregate multiple loading cases into a single optimization objective using a p-norm.
Base cells used include simple four-rod cubic lattices and more complex geometries, demonstrating method versatility.
Finite element analysis assumes linear elasticity and plane stress conditions with strains around 1%.
The cloak design enables introducing voids without affecting structural integrity or functionality.
The method outperforms existing parametric and lattice transformation approaches in versatility and performance.
Potential applications include soft robotics and implant design requiring heterogeneous mechanical properties.
The study provides a general framework for multiscale optimization of functional mechanical metamaterials.
